nameStory: The 'toothed' in this spider's name likely refers to tiny projections on the male's mouthparts (chelicerae) that help distinguish it from other slender jumping spiders. Like other jumping spiders in the genus Marpissa, it gets the 'slender' part of its name from its elongated, narrow body shape that's quite different from the compact, chunky build of most other jumping spiders.
description: The Toothed Slender Jumping Spider is a small, elongated jumping spider with the characteristic forward-facing eyes and excellent vision typical of its family. Unlike the compact, robust bodies of most jumping spiders, this species has a noticeably stretched-out appearance. It's quite small, typically measuring less than half an inch in body length. As a jumping spider, it doesn't build webs to catch prey but instead actively hunts by stalking and pouncing on small insects.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly elongated and narrow body that feels almost tube-like compared to other jumping spiders - imagine a typical chunky jumping spider that's been gently stretched lengthwise

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large forward-facing front eyes that seem almost too big for the narrow face, giving it an alert, curious expression typical of jumping spiders

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider with body length typically under 6mm, about the size of a grain of rice or smaller

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in the characteristic stop-and-go pattern of jumping spiders, often turning its whole body to look directly at you with those big front eyes

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Generally brown or grayish coloration with subtle patterns that can vary, but the overall slender profile is more distinctive than specific markings

habitat: Based on its known range extending into northern areas like Ontario, this spider likely inhabits wooded areas, possibly on tree bark or among leaf litter where its slender build helps it navigate tight spaces. In New England, look for it in deciduous and mixed forests, particularly on tree trunks or fallen logs where it can hunt for small prey.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning their hunting season after overwintering in protected locations like under bark or in leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be spotted actively hunting during daylight hours, especially on warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Mating season occurs, with females potentially laying egg sacs in sheltered locations before cold weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Spiders seek shelter under bark, in rock crevices, or deep in leaf litter to survive freezing temperatures in a dormant state.

funFact: This spider is so rare in New England that it has only been documented once in the entire region, making any sighting a potentially significant scientific observation worth reporting to local naturalist groups!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other slender jumping spiders in the Marpissa genus, but the Toothed Slender Jumping Spider's specific identification often requires close examination of male mouthpart structures. Remember: if it's a slender jumping spider in New England, it's much more likely to be one of the more common Marpissa species unless you're looking at preserved specimens under magnification.
contextualKnowledge: The extremely low observation count in New England (just one recorded sighting) suggests this species may be at the northern edge of its range here, or it could be easily overlooked due to its small size and secretive habits on tree bark.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives like the Four-lined Slender Jumping Spider, the Toothed Slender Jumping Spider lacks the distinctive light stripes that make other Marpissa species easier to identify in the field. The Pike Slender Jumper and other genus members share the same basic elongated body plan, making species-level identification challenging without examining fine details of the male's specialized mouthpart structures.

Unlike its relative the Pike Slender Jumper which has more mottled markings, the Four-lined consistently shows those four pale stripes.

Among the slender jumping spiders in its genus, the Pike Slender Jumper can be distinguished from the Four-lined Slender Jumping Spider by lacking the distinctive parallel lines on its body, and from the Toothed Slender Jumping Spider by its smoother body profile.
